data.title: Seňa – Várhely, a lost Slavic stronghold south of Košice
data.excerpt: Štefan Kolivoško, deputy director of the J. Bocatius Public Library in Košice, reconstructs the Great Old Stronghold at Seňa from charters and old maps: a Slavic lowland stronghold whose defences ran for some 2,860 m. Nothing of it survives today — the northern rampart was bulldozed in 1962 — yet charters of 1255 and 1317 and a map of 1784 still place it between the Belžanský potok and the railway station.
data.metaTitle: Seňa – Várhely, a Slavic stronghold south of Košice
data.metaDescription: The Slavic stronghold known as the Great Old Stronghold near Seňa, south of Košice. Its site, Várhely, survived in local oral tradition into the 20th century.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: The cadastral area between the Belžanský potok stream and the railway station, south of Košice, near the Slovak–Hungarian border; Hungarian name Várhely (Slovak Hradová)

keyFacts.label: Dimensions
keyFacts.value: Assumed length of the defences 2,860 m, ramparts 9–10 m wide, height estimated at 4–5 m

keyFacts.label: Construction
keyFacts.value: Timber-and-earth rampart without a stone facing (no building stone in the surroundings), probably of grillage or box construction

keyFacts.label: Defensive features
keyFacts.value: Ditches fed by the Szartos brook (east) and the Belžanský potok (west and south); on the north, where the ditch could not be filled with water, the strongest ramparts are assumed

keyFacts.label: Estimated population
keyFacts.value: About 500–600 warriors to man the ramparts; with women, children and old people some 2,000 people in all in times of danger

keyFacts.label: Historical names
keyFacts.value: Óvár and Nagyóvár (Old Stronghold and Great Old Stronghold) in the earliest charters; related cadastral names Fidvár (Kechnec) and Sárvár (Gyňov)

keyFacts.label: Author of the text
keyFacts.value: Štefan Kolivoško, deputy director of the J. Bocatius Public Library in Košice; illustrations by Ing. Peter Zdravecký

timeline.title: Assumed origin of the Great Old Stronghold
timeline.description: An early Slavic tribal stronghold, the centre of a wide region; its origin is placed before the 10th century, since permanent fortified places arise only once the population is permanently settled.

timeline.title: The period when the stronghold was in use
timeline.description: The upper chronological limit for the founding of the stronghold — the period when the Old Great Stronghold still served as the central stronghold of a wide area.

timeline.title: Founding of the New Stronghold at Abaújvár
timeline.description: The New Stronghold came into being before King Samuel Aba's accession to the throne (1041–1044); by then the Old Great Stronghold was evidently no longer usable and militarily obsolete.

timeline.title: The New Stronghold takes over the central role
timeline.description: After the New Stronghold (Abaújvár) was built, it became the administrative and political centre of the county in place of the Great Old Stronghold.

timeline.title: The first written mention
timeline.description: King Béla IV granted the land of Čaňa (Chon) to the people of Seňa; in describing the boundaries, the deed of donation mentions a place called Ówár (Old Stronghold).

timeline.title: Metatio of the Kechnec–Seňa boundary
timeline.description: The charter on the marking out of the northern boundaries of Kechnec mentions the lower end of the stronghold called Nagyowar (Great Old Stronghold).

timeline.title: Map of Seňa and its surroundings
timeline.description: A map found in the Hadtörténeti Múzeum (the Museum of Military History) in Budapest shows the ramparts of the Great Old Stronghold in their entirety.

timeline.title: Surveys of the ramparts
timeline.description: The maps of G. Györffy and M. Lamiová record the ramparts in the form of a trapezium — the northern side about 670 m long, the distance between the north and south ramparts 870 m, the southern rampart about 450 m, the ramparts 9–10 m wide and 1 m high.

timeline.title: Destruction of the northern part of the rampart
timeline.description: During construction work the northern part of the rampart was pushed flat by a bulldozer; the southern part merged with the surrounding ground as a result of cultivation.

timeline.title: Varsík's location of the stronghold
timeline.description: Branislav Varsík located the stronghold on the rise between the Belžanský potok and the Szartos brook — but archaeological survey found no traces of fortification at this place.

children.text: Mr Štefan Kolivoško, deputy director of the J. Bocatius Public Library in Košice and a writer, has kindly provided our site with his excellent article on the Slavic hillfort of Seňa (south of Košice, on the Slovak–Hungarian border). Our warm thanks go to him for his willingness. The illustrations are the work of Ing. Peter Zdravecký.
THE GREAT OLD FORT

The cadastral area in Seňa between the Belžanský potok stream and the railway station is known under the Hungarian name Várhely (Hradová, the place of the stronghold). This name lived on in Seňa in oral tradition until the 1970s. The name Várhely can be traced on cadastral maps throughout the 19th century, and also on special military maps of the 20th century. For at least 150 years the area has been depicted under the name Várhely. The name itself indicates that a stronghold once stood at this place. Today, however, nothing suggests that a stronghold stood here in the past. The site is built over by a farm belonging to the agricultural cooperative.

Did a stronghold really stand here, or is this merely a chance name? In the book Osídlenie košickej kotliny (The Settlement of the Košice Basin) by the well-known Slovak historian Branislav Varsík we can find the following information on the question of the Seňa stronghold (vol. I, p. 25). "Let us look in this connection at the immediate surroundings of Abaújvár (Novum Castrum), which arose under King Samuel Aba (1041–1044) already as a royal stronghold, while the older Slavic tribal stronghold lay on the other side of the Hornád on a rise to the north-east of Seňa". The archaeologists Bánesz and Lamiová likewise have no doubt that the stronghold existed, but they place it somewhere other than Varsík does.

Archival documents testify unambiguously in favour of the stronghold's existence. The first written mention we know of is from 1255. King Béla IV granted the land of Čaňa (Chon) to the people of Seňa. In the deed of donation, as was then the custom, he describes the boundaries of the granted land. Part of the boundary of the land reached as far as the area called Ówár (Old Stronghold). A further mention is from 1317. The charter concerns a metatio – the marking out of the northern boundaries of Kechnec. These are therefore the boundaries between the cadastral areas of Seňa and Kechnec. In the book already mentioned, Varsík gives a free account of the results of the metatio: "The northern boundaries of the Kechnec cadastral area were then marked out as follows: they begin in the west at the dead arm of the river Ida called Holtida (in 1251, in the description of the boundaries of Bočiar, this arm is still given as Mortua aqua Ida, that is, still by its Slovak name) and from there they ran east along the road that exists to this day, as far as the village of Seňa itself: at the southern edge of the village of Seňa the boundary crossed the great road (this is the great road that led from the south to Košice and on to the Torysa) and continued east to the Belžanský potok (ad rivulum Belzepataka vocatum) and, after crossing this stream, reached the lower end of the stronghold called Nagyowar (pervenit ad inferiorem finem castri Nagyowar dictum)".

Cadastral names relating to the stronghold survived not only in Seňa but also in the surrounding villages. In Kechnec the fields bordering on Várhely were called Fidvár, which is probably the original Hungarian name Földvár (Earthen Stronghold). In the cadastral area of the neighbouring village of Gyňov the local name Sárvár (Muddy Stronghold) occurs. We have already mentioned that the opinions of specialists differ as to the precise location and size of the Seňa stronghold. In 1951 Varsík placed it on "...an extensive rise in the middle of the plain between the Belžanský potok and the Szartos brook, or, in terms of villages, between Belža and Gyňov. This stronghold occupies the whole rise, which extends above the 208 m contour line, and its length from north to south was as much as 3–4 km and its width from west to east over 1 km.

The existence of this stronghold and its extent are confirmed for us by the oldest charters concerning this region, in which this stronghold is mentioned in the descriptions of the boundaries of Čaňa and Felnémeti and is given already in Hungarian, as Óvár and Nagyóvár, that is, as Old Stronghold and Great Old Stronghold". Varsík locates the northern boundary of the stronghold on the basis of the above-mentioned deed of donation of Béla IV from 1255. "He grants the land of Čaňa (Chon) to the guests from Seňa (de Scynna), and on this occasion the boundaries of this land are described; in the south-west they reached as far as the upper part of the place called Old Stronghold (Ówár). Specifically, it is stated here that from the river Szartos the boundary of the land of Čaňa runs south to a large poplar and from there extends as far as the southern part of the place (that is, the boundary of the land of Čaňa went only as far as the slope of the rise) called Ówár. This was a place to the north-west of Gyňov, where the boundary of Čaňa reached the slope of the original Old Stronghold". Varsík places the southern part of the stronghold approximately 800 m north of the Seňa railway station. In locating the stronghold Varsík relied on archival documents that did not concern the stronghold directly.

children.text: Mária Lamiová and Ladislav Bánesz chose a different approach. They tackled the problem from an archaeological and topographical point of view. Their conclusions regarding the location and size of the stronghold are different. In his study B. Varsík identified Óvár as the hill that runs from north to south above the village of Belža and is bounded by the Szartos and Belžanský streams. It is a place that at first sight appears to be the strategically most important in the area, and which therefore naturally gives the impression that the stronghold must have stood here.

Archaeological surveys in the cadastral area of Seňa, however, established that there are no traces of a hillfort on the hill itself. All that could be found here were traces of earlier prehistoric occupation, without any remains of fortification. In the places where Varsík located the stronghold, therefore, no material evidence was found. Where, then, did the Great Old Stronghold lie? While studying documents we came across a special military map of the General Staff of the Austro-Hungarian army from the last century. On the map one can follow a rise in the ground along the road from the Belžanský potok to the railway station. It is of interest that a right-angled termination of the rise can be observed on the map. Some 800 m further south, another rise in the ground is shown on the map, parallel to the previous one. We assumed that these were the remains of the ramparts of the Great Old Stronghold.

Our assumption was supported by G. Györffy's publication Az árpád - kori Magyarország történeti földrajza (The Historical Geography of Hungary in the Árpád Period). In connection with the Old Great Stronghold he also refers to maps of 1880–91, on which the ramparts are shown in the form of a square. To be more precise than Györffy, it is rather a trapezium, adapted to the natural conditions of the place. According to Lamiová's survey its northern side runs roughly along the road from the Belžanský potok to the railway station and is about 670 m long; the distance between the north and south ramparts is 870 m. The length of the rampart on the south is around 450 m. She gives the width of the ramparts as 9–10 m and the height as 1 m.

Today the ramparts no longer exist even in the form in which they were described more than forty years ago. During construction work in 1962 the northern part of the rampart was pushed flat by a bulldozer. The southern part of the rampart merged with the surrounding ground as a result of intensive cultivation. The eastern rampart is partly indicated on the map mentioned above. Of the western rampart there is no trace either on the map or in the field. We believe that, on the basis of our research in the documents, we can unambiguously confirm Lamiová's hypothesis as against Varsík's. In the Hadtörténeti Múzeum (the Museum of Military History) in Budapest we succeeded in finding a map of Seňa and its surroundings from 1784, on which the ramparts of the Great Old Stronghold are shown in their entirety at the place where Lamiová locates them. We do not know the precise period in which the Great Old Stronghold at Seňa came into being. We do, however, have relatively precise reports on the founding of the New Stronghold at Abaújvár. The New Stronghold was founded before the accession of King Samuel Aba (1041–1044) to the throne. This probably happened after the death of King Stephen I (1038). The Old Great Stronghold was evidently by then no longer usable and militarily obsolete.
Varsík
likewise does not date the time when the Old Great Stronghold came into being. He does, however, clearly

speak of an early Slavic tribal stronghold that was the centre of a wide region. The origin of the stronghold can therefore be put back before the 10th century, with the 9th and the beginning of the 10th century taken as the upper chronological limit for its founding. The 7th–8th century may be regarded as the lower chronological limit

. Permanent fortified places only come into being at a time when we can speak of a permanently settled population, and not during the Migration Period. Permanent fortified places arose only once ownership of a given territory had been recognised and the population had become anchored in it. The building of a stronghold could be undertaken only once part of the population no longer had to take direct part in cultivating the land.

Our ideas about castles are formed on the basis of what we know of castles built after the 13th century. The Great Old Stronghold was fundamentally different. In his book Staroslovanské hradisko (The Early Slavic Hillfort) Miloš Šolle quotes the account of the Jewish merchant and traveller Ibrahim ibn Yaqub, who visited the Slavic lands in the 10th century and described the way in which the Slavs built their strongholds. The merchant and traveller writes as follows: "Most of their strongholds the Slavs build in this way: they go out to meadows rich in water and scrub, mark out with stakes a round or rectangular area to the size of the stronghold they intend to build, dig a ditch all around it and pile up the excavated earth, reinforcing it with hurdles and posts in the manner of bastions until the rampart reaches the required height. On the side where they want the entrance to the stronghold to be, they measure out the gateway of the stronghold, and there one then enters and leaves the stronghold by a wooden bridge". The quotation given above is in fact the basic scheme for building a stronghold in the lowlands, and we may therefore assume that the Seňa stronghold was built in a similar way.

First of all, then, the ditches were dug and the rampart was piled up from the earth obtained. In the Classic Hillfort period, to which the Great Old Stronghold can probably be assigned, two kinds of rampart were built – timber-and-earth ramparts without a stone facing, or timber-and-earth ramparts with a stone facing. Since no stones of any great weight occur in Seňa or its immediate surroundings, it may be assumed that the stronghold had timber-and-earth ramparts without a stone facing. The ramparts had a respectable width of 9–10 metres. We do not know their exact height, but from the width alone it may be inferred that they reached at least 4–5 m. If the rampart was to keep its shape and strength and not quickly give way to the weather, it was necessary to use the technique of grillage or box ramparts. Timbers were laid across the rampart and formed a kind of grillage, which was filled in with earth. If so-called boxes were formed from the timbers and these were filled with earth, we speak of the box type of fortification.

From the point of view of defence the stronghold was placed in a very good position. On the eastern side the Szartos brook flowed past it, and on the western side the Belžanský potok. There is no doubt that these two watercourses were used for the stronghold's defence. It can be asserted with almost complete certainty that the stronghold's ditches were filled with water on the eastern, western and also the southern side. Given the difference in ground level, the ditches on the northern side could not be filled with water, and we therefore assume that the strongest ramparts of the stronghold stood here.

No written documents have survived about the inhabitants of the stronghold and their number. From the extent of the ramparts, from their total length, we can reach certain conclusions about the number of the stronghold's inhabitants. In defending the stronghold's ramparts it was necessary to reckon with one man for every 5-metre stretch. Had the defence been thinner, the enemy could have taken the stronghold relatively easily, even though we assume the possibility of regrouping towards the points of fiercest attack and the weakest points of the defence, which were the entrances and gates. The assumed length of the defences was 2,860 metres. For such a long circuit it was necessary, in the event of fighting, to field at least 500–600 warriors. The total number of inhabitants, however, was considerably higher. To the number of warriors must be added at least three times as many non-combatant women, children and old people. In this way we arrive at a figure of about 2,000 inhabitants of the stronghold. The number of inhabitants in times of peace was considerably lower. A long-term concentration of a large number of people on half a square kilometre would necessarily have led to a shortage of space for building dwellings and farm structures. In times of danger the inhabitants sought not only their own safety but also that of their movable property and livestock. We may therefore conclude that the stronghold had a permanent garrison of a smaller number of warriors and that in times of danger their numbers were made up from the men who took shelter behind the stronghold's ramparts from the surrounding settlements.

Varsík regards the Great Old Stronghold as the central stronghold of a wide area. He connects it with the fortified places at Barca, which were to prevent enemies from penetrating from the north along the main road of the Košice Basin. It should be noted that the Great Road (we write about it in another chapter) ran on the right bank of the Hornád until the New Stronghold (Abaújvár) came into being. A similar role to that of Barca was played in the south by the fortification at Garadna. According to Varsík this is indicated by the name Garadna (Hradná?) itself and by the local name Sárvár (Muddy Stronghold). After the New Stronghold (Újvár – Abaújvár) was built, it was this stronghold that took over the function of central stronghold from the Great Old Stronghold. It became the administrative and political centre of the county. In the early history of the Kingdom of Hungary it drew attention to itself several times, whether in connection with King Samuel Aba or with the princes Andrew and Levente. These historical events, however, no longer have any direct connection with the Great Old Stronghold."
